title: Anthropic's FlashProve Can Prove Which AI Model Wrote an Answer
excerpt: The open-source prototype uses zero-knowledge cryptography to guarantee an AI response came from the model you asked for — without revealing that model's secret weights.
body:
• Anthropic has released FlashProve, an open-source prototype that cryptographically proves a response came from a specific AI model, using a technique called provable inference.
  • On a 400-billion-parameter Llama 4 Maverick model, one H100 GPU generates proofs at about 110 tokens per second — at roughly 70 to 95 times the computing cost of running the model itself.
  • The proof hides the model's weights, so commercial labs could let customers and regulators verify which model answered them without exposing proprietary technology.
  • Anthropic stresses this is intermediate research: it has released code, a technical report and formal proofs under Apache 2.0, and says there are no plans to deploy FlashProve at any lab.

When you ask an AI chatbot a question, you have no way of knowing whether the model you selected actually produced the answer — a routing service could quietly substitute a cheaper model, or an attacker could tamper with the response. Anthropic has released an open-source system aimed at closing that gap. FlashProve, detailed in a research post on Anthropic's site, attaches a cryptographic proof to a model's output: a mathematical guarantee that a specific model generated that response.

""This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda," the researchers write."

How the proof works

FlashProve is built on a cryptographic object called a zkSNARK. The provider first publishes a commitment — a short fingerprint of one exact set of model weights — while the weights themselves stay secret. For each response, the provider then generates a proof that the committed weights produced that output from that input. Anyone can check the proof quickly on an ordinary computer, and if a different model, or altered arithmetic, produced the response, the check fails. Because the proof is zero-knowledge, it reveals nothing about the weights themselves — the asset closed-model makers such as Anthropic and OpenAI guard most closely.

https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2117710942826123294

TechCrunch, which reported the release on Tuesday, compared the idea to cryptographic email signatures: a way for a recipient to confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, robust even against the lab that built the model. The system could stop a company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive one to inflate benchmark results, the researchers note.

Fast enough to matter, costly enough to limit

The headline numbers come from a demanding test case: Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 4-bit quantized weights. A single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens per second, with a proof size of about 19 MB per 1,024-token request. The catch is overhead: proving takes roughly 70 to 95 times the GPU time of simply running the model on vLLM, a common open-source serving library. Anthropic also notes the current system proves an integer-arithmetic version of the model, and verification of its formal security guarantees is provided in Lean, a formal verification language — the team published machine-checked proofs of the protocol's top-level security statements alongside a fast C++ verifier for routine use.

Anthropic is candid that the work is unfinished. "This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda," the researchers write. "We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it." TechCrunch reports there are no plans to deploy the system at Anthropic or any other lab.

Why regulators and customers care

Anthropic lays out four problems provable inference could address: regulators who need to confirm a provider's hardware is serving approved models rather than training new ones; tamper detection, where a compromised server or a substituted model could not forge proofs for the expected weights; text provenance, letting a company verify a claim that a frontier model really performed a security scan or review; and model approval, where a regulator could require proofs that only approved models are being served. The release includes the technical report, a protocol specification, executable code and the Lean proofs, all under the Apache 2.0 license.

One detail Anthropic flags itself: much of the optimization work behind FlashProve was done by its own model, Claude — and, as the team puts it, Claude often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, which is precisely why the security claims are backed by formal, auditable proofs rather than by trust in the code.
